description: Infrastructure and deployments are defined as code / automated, not manual console changes.
evidence: HashiCorp Terraform acts as the definitive Infrastructure as Code (IaC) standard.

description: Monitoring, logging, and alerting are defined for the workload's key operational signals.
evidence: AWS CloudWatch and Prometheus/Grafana handle all metric collection and alerting.

description: An incident response process or runbook is referenced for operational failures.
evidence: Any P1/P2 system failures trigger automated PagerDuty runbooks.

description: Changes can be rolled back safely; deployment approach limits blast radius of a bad change.
evidence: application container deployments to EKS are currently executed manually via kubectl apply commands from a centralized bastion jump-box by the lead developer.

description: IAM roles/permissions follow least privilege rather than broad/wildcard access.
evidence: IAM roles enforce strict least privilege.

description: Sensitive or PII-bearing data stores have encryption at rest specified.
evidence: Aurora databases are encrypted at rest with AWS KMS.

description: Data in transit is encrypted (TLS) between components, especially over public networks.
evidence: Data in transit is secured via TLS 1.2 externally and mTLS internally between pods.

description: Credentials/API keys/secrets are managed via a secrets store, not hardcoded or embedded in config.
evidence: AWS Secrets Manager securely stores and automatically rotates all database and payment gateway credentials.

description: Network boundaries/segmentation are defined; public-facing components are minimized and fronted appropriately.
evidence: The network perimeter is guarded by AWS WAF and Shield Advanced. EKS nodes and databases sit in private subnets with strict Security Groups.

description: Authentication/authorization (SSO, MFA, RBAC) is defined for user- and system-facing access.
evidence: Identity management utilizes OAuth2 via Auth0 for customer and system-level API access.

description: Security-relevant actions and access are logged in an auditable, tamper-resistant way.
evidence: Dedicated, tamper-resistant security audit logging (e.g., CloudTrail log file validation or centralized SIEM forwarding) is not currently implemented.

description: Critical components have redundancy (multi-AZ or equivalent) rather than a single point of failure.
evidence: EKS nodes and Aurora instances span 3 Availability Zones.

description: A disaster recovery approach with defined RTO/RPO is present for critical data/workloads.
evidence: Aurora read replicas in our secondary region guarantee an RPO of 5 minutes and an RTO of 15 minutes.

description: Dependent-service failures are isolated (retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, dead-letter queues) rather than cascading.
evidence: We utilize Resilience4j to implement strict circuit breakers and timeouts, ensuring third-party payment gateway outages do not cascade into our core systems.

description: A backup strategy exists for stateful data with a defined restore process.
evidence: Automated continuous backups and nightly RDS snapshots are enabled and tested monthly.

description: Compute/storage choices match the actual workload pattern (e.g., serverless for spiky load) rather than over-provisioning.
evidence: asynchronous nightly financial settlement reconciliation jobs still run on fixed, oversized legacy Amazon EC2 m5.4xlarge instances that run 24/7.

description: Caching is used where repeated reads or expensive computations would otherwise recur.
evidence: Amazon ElastiCache for Redis stores ephemeral cart session data to prevent expensive and repeated database reads.

description: The database/storage type matches its access pattern (e.g., not using a relational store for pure key-value lookups at scale).
evidence: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Global Database, perfectly aligning with the ACID compliance required for financial transactions.

description: Content/data delivery accounts for geographic distribution of users where relevant (CDN or regional deployment).
evidence: CloudFront caches static product assets globally.

description: Cost tracking/tagging/budgets are defined so spend is attributable and boundable.
evidence: Cost Explorer tagging (Project: GlobalCheckout) is strictly mandated on all AWS resources.

description: Resources scale down/to zero with demand rather than running at fixed capacity for variable load.
evidence: EKS Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) manages burst traffic elastically.

description: Storage has a lifecycle/retention policy rather than indefinite accumulation at full-cost tiers.
evidence: Amazon S3 Lifecycle rules are rigorously configured to transition aged order receipt blobs to S3 Glacier Deep Archive

description: Provisioning model (on-demand vs reserved/provisioned) matches the workload's actual usage predictability.
evidence: We use 3-year Reserved Instances (RIs) to cover the predictable baseline database load.

description: Managed/serverless services are used where feasible to improve utilization over self-managed idle infrastructure.
evidence: The core business logic runs on Java Spring Boot microservices inside Amazon EKS.

description: Data retention/storage footprint is minimized to what's needed rather than retained indefinitely by default.
evidence: ultimately delete them after 7 years to minimize data footprint.

description: Region/deployment choice shows awareness of energy/carbon considerations where it doesn't conflict with other constraints.
evidence: No mention of region selection based on energy or carbon considerations.
